key_insight: LLM scientific claim verifiers often reach judgments from hidden interpretations, and making those interpretations explicit with Claim Cards exposes that many verdict changes come from wording choices rather than evidence.
engineering_relevance: For AI research agents and benchmark design, the paper shows that recording the assumed interpretation alongside each verdict can improve traceability, debugging, and evaluation of claim verification systems.
method: Defined Claim Cards with 9 pre-evidence fields; each field is marked as stated, inferred, or default.
Ran a GPT-5.4 agent 5 times on each of 60 expert-labeled materials-science and biomedical claims in three settings: with a card, without a card, and with a frozen card.
Perturbed one card field at a time to test how interpretation changes affect verdicts and tool use.
evidence_signal: Across 900 runs, over 40% of card fields were not stated, the card added about 10% to tokens and time, and deliberate edits changed verdicts on about one-third of claims versus about one-seventh expected by chance (p < 0.001).
watch_item: The results come from a specific GPT-5.4 setup and a limited 60-claim benchmark, so broader generalization to other models, domains, and verifier pipelines still needs testing.
paper_title: Same Claim, Different Interpretations: How LLM Agents Resolve Ambiguity in Scientific Claims
